title: Build AI Practice Loops So Students Get 5x The Reps Without 5x Your Grading
author: Doan Winkel
summary: Doan Winkel argues that teachers assign too little meaningful practice because feedback is a grading bottleneck, and proposes AI practice loops as the fix. In a loop the student makes an unaided attempt, receives narrow AI critique that checks basics without solving, revises, and answers short reflection questions before the teacher ever grades. He gives concrete loops for writing, math, coding and language learning, guardrails against AI ghostwriting, a reusable reflection set, and a one-assignment pilot plan. The newsletter also includes ready-made prompts and a classroom rollout script. It is a practical build-guide for teachers rather than a general discussion of AI.
points: Students typically get three to five practice reps of a skill that needs twenty because every rep feels like something the teacher must grade.
The AI's job in the loop is to critique and ask questions, never to give answers or rewrite the student's work.
Students must make an unaided attempt first, and reflection questions make their use of AI feedback visible.
Narrow, single-skill targets and tight limits on what the AI may comment on keep the loop effective.
Piloting on one assignment and checking whether errors, grading load and confidence improve prevents overreach.
quotes: You’re grading the skill on a later assignment. The loops are the training block, not the competition.
You never saw the first draft. You might only see the revised intro plus their one sentence reflection.
Most students already have AI open when they code. They’re just hiding it from you.
The AI is here to react to your work, not to write it for you. If you copy paragraphs or solutions straight from ChatGPT, that’s the same as copying from a classmate.
If you build even one loop, run it honestly, and look at the reflections, you’ll learn more about your students’ thinking than from another hundred lonely grading hours.
